content_voiceover: This slide gives you the overview of pediatric brain tumors that you need for boards. On the left, the classic Nelson's diagram breaks hemispheric tumors down into gliomas, which make up thirty seven percent, split into low grade astrocytomas at twenty three percent and high grade astrocytomas at eleven percent. In the midline, chiasmal gliomas run about four percent, craniopharyngiomas eight percent, and pineal region tumors two percent. In the posterior fossa, you have four roughly equal big hitters, brainstem gliomas, medulloblastomas, and cerebellar astrocytomas each around fifteen percent, with ependymomas at four percent. On the right is a Taiwanese cohort pie chart showing low grade gliomas as the single largest group at thirty two percent, followed by germ cell tumors fourteen percent, medulloblastoma thirteen percent, high grade glioma nine percent, and craniopharyngioma eight percent. The high yield takeaway for boards is that posterior fossa tumors dominate childhood, while low grade gliomas are actually the most common single histology overall, and medulloblastoma and pineal region tumors are the two entries highlighted here because they come up repeatedly in exam questions.
keypoints: Gliomas are the most common hemispheric brain tumor category, thirty seven percent
Posterior fossa tumors, brainstem glioma, medulloblastoma, cerebellar astrocytoma, each about fifteen percent
Low grade glioma is the single most common histology overall, around thirty two percent
Medulloblastoma and pineal region tumors are exam favorites
keypoint_voiceover: Remember three things for boards. Gliomas dominate the hemispheres at thirty seven percent. The posterior fossa is split roughly evenly between brainstem glioma, medulloblastoma, and cerebellar astrocytoma. And across all locations, low grade glioma is the single most common pediatric brain tumor type.
